title: Commercial Public Adjuster in Galveston: Business Claims Help
description: Need a commercial public adjuster in Galveston? Learn how business property and business interruption claims work and how to protect your company's claim.
html:
When a hurricane, windstorm, or fire shuts down a Galveston business, the insurance claim becomes one of the most important financial events in the company's history. A commercial public adjuster represents the business owner, not the insurance company, and handles the documentation and negotiation needed for property damage, inventory, equipment, and business interruption losses. This guide explains how commercial claims differ from homeowners claims, what business interruption coverage actually requires, and how to prepare your business to file a strong claim.

What a Commercial Public Adjuster Does

A commercial public adjuster is licensed in Texas by the Texas Department of Insurance (TDI) and works on behalf of the policyholder. On a business claim, that typically includes:

  • Reviewing the commercial property policy, endorsements, and any separate windstorm or flood policies
  • Documenting building damage, improvements and betterments, equipment, and inventory
  • Preparing a detailed repair estimate that reflects current local construction costs and code requirements
  • Working with your accountant to calculate business income loss and extra expense
  • Presenting the claim and negotiating with the insurer's adjusters, accountants, and consultants

The insurer will usually bring its own team, which may include building consultants, engineers, and forensic accountants. A commercial public adjuster gives the business its own coordinated team.

Commercial Claims on the Galveston Coast

Galveston businesses face some unique issues:

  • Split coverage. Many coastal commercial properties carry windstorm coverage through TWIA and a separate commercial policy for other perils, plus flood coverage. Figuring out which policy pays for which damage is critical. See our TWIA claims help page for more on windstorm coverage.
  • Wind vs. water. After a hurricane, carriers may argue whether damage came from wind, wind-driven rain, or storm surge.
  • Code and elevation requirements. Repairs to older buildings can trigger current code and floodplain requirements. Ordinance or law coverage may matter. Our Galveston local code page outlines local requirements.
  • Seasonal revenue. Tourism-driven businesses on the Island have strong seasonal swings, which complicates business interruption calculations.

Business Interruption Coverage Explained

Business interruption, often called business income coverage, is designed to replace the income your business loses while it cannot operate because of covered physical damage. It generally includes:

  • Lost net income the business would have earned during the restoration period
  • Continuing normal operating expenses, such as payroll (depending on the policy), rent, loan payments, and utilities
  • Extra expense to reduce the shutdown, such as temporary locations, equipment rentals, or expedited shipping

Key policy terms to find and understand:

  • Waiting period: Many policies do not pay for the first 48 or 72 hours of shutdown. Check yours.
  • Period of restoration: How long the policy will pay, often tied to how long repairs should reasonably take.
  • Extended period of indemnity: Additional time after reopening while revenue recovers, if purchased.
  • Civil authority coverage: Coverage when a government order prevents access, such as after a hurricane evacuation, subject to policy conditions.
  • Coinsurance: If business income limits were set too low, a penalty may reduce payment.

Important: business interruption usually requires direct physical loss or damage from a covered peril. If the building was damaged by an excluded cause, the income loss tied to that damage may not be covered under that policy.

Documents Your Business Should Gather

Business income claims are proven with records. Start collecting:

  1. Profit and loss statements for at least the prior two to three years, monthly if possible
  2. Tax returns and sales tax reports
  3. Payroll records
  4. Budgets and forecasts prepared before the loss
  5. Bank statements
  6. Inventory records and purchase invoices
  7. Equipment lists with purchase dates and costs
  8. Leases, including who is responsible for improvements
  9. Receipts for every extra expense after the loss
  10. Photos and video of damage, before any cleanup where safe

Step-by-Step: Handling a Commercial Property Claim

  1. Report the claim to every potentially applicable insurer. Windstorm, commercial property, and flood. TWIA claims must be reported within one year of the date of loss, and other policies require prompt notice.
  2. Protect the property and mitigate. Tarp, board up, extract water, and move salvageable inventory. Keep all receipts.
  3. Document before you discard. Photograph damaged inventory and equipment and keep samples if possible until the insurer has had a chance to inspect.
  4. Track extra expenses separately. Set up a dedicated account code or spreadsheet for post-loss costs.
  5. Get a repair estimate that reflects reality. Commercial construction costs on the Island can differ from generic pricing.
  6. Build the business income claim with your accountant. Use historical data and seasonality to show what the business would have earned.
  7. Submit in writing and track deadlines. The Texas Prompt Payment of Claims Act, Insurance Code chapter 542, sets timelines insurers must follow.
  8. Request partial payments. For large losses, ask about advances or partial payments on undisputed amounts to keep the business afloat.

How a Commercial Public Adjuster Works With Your Team

A commercial public adjuster does not replace your accountant, attorney, or contractor. Instead, the adjuster coordinates the claim so each professional's work fits together. Your accountant supplies the financial records and helps model lost income. Your contractor or building consultant helps confirm repair scope and timeline, which directly affects the period of restoration. The commercial public adjuster translates all of that into a claim presentation that follows the policy language, submits it, answers the insurer's questions, and negotiates the numbers. For multi-location businesses, landlords with tenants, or owners with separate wind and flood policies, this coordination can prevent gaps where one policy points to another and nothing gets paid.

It also frees the owner to focus on employees, customers, and reopening. In the weeks after a Gulf Coast storm, that time matters.

Common Mistakes Business Owners Make

  • Waiting to file while trying to clean up and reopen
  • Throwing out damaged inventory before documenting it
  • Letting the insurer's accountant define the business income loss without your own analysis
  • Forgetting tenant improvements and betterments
  • Not claiming extra expenses that shortened the shutdown
  • Accepting a restoration period that is shorter than repairs will realistically take

Does Your Business Need a Commercial Public Adjuster?

Not every business loss needs a commercial public adjuster. Smaller, simple losses can sometimes be handled directly. Consider professional representation when:

  • The business is closed or partially closed
  • More than one policy may apply
  • The insurer has hired engineers or forensic accountants
  • You are managing repairs, employees, and customers and do not have time to run the claim
  • The insurer's estimate or business income calculation seems low

A commercial public adjuster cannot guarantee a particular result, but can make sure the claim is fully documented and presented. You can also review past storms that affected local businesses on our Galveston storm history page.

faq.q: What does a commercial public adjuster do?
faq.a: A commercial public adjuster, licensed by the Texas Department of Insurance, represents a business owner on a property insurance claim, documenting building, inventory, equipment, and business income losses and negotiating with the insurer.

faq.q: Does business interruption insurance cover hurricane closures in Galveston?
faq.a: It may, if the closure results from direct physical damage by a covered peril and policy conditions such as waiting periods are met. Civil authority coverage may apply to evacuation orders depending on the policy language.

faq.q: What records do I need for a business interruption claim?
faq.a: Profit and loss statements, tax returns, payroll records, bank statements, budgets, and receipts for extra expenses are commonly needed to prove lost income and costs.
